A1.notes.Q3: I use course data daily, but tracking login activity feels like surveillance. We must be careful not to penalize students with external responsibilities just because they study off-campus.
A1.notes.Q4: As an advisor, I cannot explain a 'black box' decision to a distressed student. If I can't articulate the 'why', my intervention loses credibility and trust.
A1.notes.Q5: We cannot afford to miss vulnerable students from specific backgrounds just to make the model statistically perfect for everyone. Missing those who need help is worse than contacting a few extra.
A1.notes.Q6: Generic emails are easily ignored by students in crisis. A personalized invitation to talk is more effective, but timing matters; we must reach them before it's too late.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic info, casting a wider net is safe. For personalized outreach, which takes my time and feels intrusive, we need more precision to avoid overwhelming students or wasting resources.
A1.Q8.1: The human element is missing from this model. A predictive flag cannot replace the nuanced understanding of a student's personal crisis that an experienced advisor develops through conversation.

A2.notes.Q3: Course performance is useful, but I distrust administrative history and reject all surveillance data like Absalon logs or demographics. The 'panopticon' effect undermines trust.
A2.notes.Q4: As an advisor, I cannot justify a decision to a student without understanding the 'why'. Black-box models destroy my ability to build trust and offer real help.
A2.notes.Q5: I'd accept losing some reach to ensure non-dominant groups aren't missed. Our priority is catching those at risk, not minimizing false alarms for the well-adjusted.
A2.notes.Q6: Automated emails often feel cold; a personalized note followed by a voluntary meeting is far more effective for engagement in my experience.
A2.notes.Q7: For generic info, cast a wide net safely. For personal messages referencing specific struggles, I must be extremely precise to avoid invasive errors.
A2.Q8.1: We need robust opt-out mechanisms where students can disable this monitoring without penalty or stigma, preserving their autonomy while keeping the safety net available for those who choose it.

A3.notes.Q3: I worry about surveillance creep with Absalon data. Course performance is fair game, but demographic data must be strictly limited to fairness corrections only.
A3.notes.Q4: I cannot explain a 'black box' decision to a distressed student. If I can't articulate the reason, I lose my ability to build trust and offer real help.
A3.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling student is worse than annoying one who doesn't need help yet. We must ensure marginalized groups aren't disproportionately missed by the net.
A3.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. I need to invite them to a real conversation before they drop out completely. Early means immediately upon detection.
A3.notes.Q7: With general info, err on the side of inclusion. With personalized outreach involving my time and their vulnerability, precision becomes more critical to avoid stigma.
A3.Q8.1: We must ensure students can opt out of data collection or at least opt out of being flagged without penalty. Autonomy is key in a welfare context.

S1.notes.Q3: Academic data helps, but I quit once before feeling watched. Adding sensitive personal details feels like surveillance unless it's strictly to catch students in my situation who are falling through cracks.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm flagged. If the reason is opaque, it feels like a black box judging me again. At least explain which credits or grades caused the alert.
S1.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help is worse than slightly lower overall numbers, especially for first-gen or financially stressed peers like I was. We can't afford to be missed twice.
S1.notes.Q6: Don't wait for the end of a semester; I didn't ask for help until it was too late. A personalized note with an option to meet would feel supportive, not judgmental.
S1.notes.Q7: For generic emails, err on the side of caution and send more. But for personal messages from advisors, be careful; I don't want to feel targeted if I'm actually fine.
S1.Q8.1: Please ensure students can easily opt out or control how their data is used for these models. The fear of being labeled 'at-risk' shouldn't discourage me from working part-time or taking breaks when needed.

S2.notes.Q3: As an international student, using my high school data or LMS tracking feels like surveillance. I only accept basic academic data if it significantly improves early help, but I reject sensitive data entirely.
S2.notes.Q4: I need to know why I am flagged. If the reason is hidden or too complex, it destroys trust. High explainability with small gains is better than a black box.
S2.notes.Q5: Failing to catch students who struggle because of bias is worse than missing a few others. We must ensure vulnerable groups aren't overlooked, even if the total number drops slightly.
S2.notes.Q6: Personalized emails or phone calls feel invasive and stigmatizing for someone just starting to struggle. A generic, low-pressure email is better. Don't call constantly; once a year is enough.
S2.notes.Q7: For general emails, cast a wide net (better safe than sorry). But for personalized messages that mention my specific struggles, I prefer being missed over having my private data shared unnecessarily.
S2.Q8.1: The model must not penalize international students who study abroad in their home country during summers or have different academic calendars. The system needs cultural context to avoid false positives based on non-EU education structures.

S3.notes.Q3: As someone with a health condition, I fear being watched by the university. Using grades or admissions is risky, but Absalon tracking feels like surveillance that destroys trust. Sensitive data must never be used.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged to trust the support offered. If a model is too complex to explain, it feels like a black box making life-altering decisions about me.
S3.notes.Q5: It is better to miss fewer struggling students if it ensures marginalized groups are not left behind by the system. Inequality in identification is harmful; we must prioritize catching those at risk.
S3.notes.Q6: A generic, low-pressure email is best. A direct call or personalized message based on private data feels invasive and shaming. Outreach should be an invitation, not a confrontation.
S3.notes.Q7: General info emails can cast a wide net safely. However, personalized interventions require high certainty; false positives here damage trust and feel like an accusation of failure.
S3.Q8.1: The biggest concern is the chilling effect on students with health conditions who might avoid registering for courses or using support services to stay off the radar. The fear of being flagged often prevents seeking help until it is too late.

S4.notes.Q3: As a student with ADHD, my late submissions are a symptom, not a character flaw. Tracking Absalon activity feels like surveillance, but disability data is crucial for early help if used ethically.
S4.notes.Q4: If I'm flagged, I need to know why to trust the system and fix it. Black boxes feel like being punished by an algorithm I can't argue with.
S4.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling student is worse than emailing someone who doesn't need help yet. We must ensure students like me aren't overlooked due to data bias against neurodivergent patterns.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic emails get deleted. I need a personal touch and an option to talk to a human advisor quickly, not just once a year when it might be too late.
S4.notes.Q7: For generic info, better to over-contact. For personalized messages, we must respect my inbox and privacy; false positives here feel invasive rather than helpful.
S4.Q8.1: The university needs to ensure advisors are trained on neurodiversity so that outreach doesn't stigmatize students like me with ADHD or other hidden disabilities.

S5.notes.Q3: I am an international student; using my nationality or origin data feels invasive and risks profiling. Performance data is okay if it truly helps, but tracking my every click on Absalon feels like surveillance unless the benefit is huge.
S5.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged, especially as a new student unfamiliar with the system. A black box model is unacceptable. If it works better but I can't ask 'why?', trust will be lost.
S5.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling international student is worse than accidentally contacting one who isn't struggling. We might not know where to get help. Equal fairness is crucial, but we can't sacrifice too many real cases.
S5.notes.Q6: As an international student, I often don't know when to ask for help. A generic email is too impersonal. A voluntary meeting invite feels supportive. Waiting until end-of-year is too late; support should be immediate.
S5.notes.Q7: It's better to send a few extra friendly messages than to miss someone who is silently struggling. False alarms are annoying but fixable; missed students might drop out before anyone notices.
S5.Q8.1: Please ensure advisors understand the cultural context of international students. Academic difficulties often stem from isolation or unfamiliar grading systems, not lack of ability. The system must be sensitive to these nuances.

S6.notes.Q3: As a non-native speaker who switched programs, I know academic struggle isn't just about grades. But tracking Absalon clicks feels invasive surveillance. Sensitive data should be banned unless it directly fixes bias against groups like international students.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know why I'm flagged, especially if I'm a foreign student. A 'black box' makes me fear bias without recourse. High explainability is crucial for trust; I won't trade much accuracy for total opacity.
S6.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling student who needs help (like me once was) hurts more than false alarms. We must prioritize catching everyone at risk, even if the model becomes slightly less efficient overall for some groups.
S6.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored; I need to feel seen, not just spammed. A personalized invite to talk with an advisor feels supportive, not policing. Help should be available immediately when struggles arise.
S6.notes.Q7: Better to annoy a few than miss the one who needs help desperately. With personalized messages, maybe we can afford slightly fewer false alarms, but I'd rather send too many invites than too few.
S6.Q8.1: The system must have an easy 'opt-out' or appeal process for students flagged unfairly due to language barriers or cultural differences in study habits.

S7.notes.Q3: Using grades is okay for accuracy, but tracking my every click on Absalon feels like surveillance. As a student with dyslexia, I fear data misuse, yet disability status could help tailor support if safeguards exist.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged to trust the system. If it's a 'black box,' I might feel targeted or misunderstood, especially regarding my disability accommodations.
S7.notes.Q5: It is vital that students with hidden disabilities like mine aren't missed. Prioritizing equal recall ensures we get the help we need, even if it means fewer false positives.
S7.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored; I need personalized outreach. Since difficulties can happen anytime, continuous monitoring ensures early support before we fall too far behind.
S7.notes.Q7: For general info, cast a wide net. For personalized messages referencing specific struggles, be more selective to avoid stigmatizing students who are actually fine.
S7.Q8.1: The model must account for the 'learning curve' of first-year students, especially those with disabilities like dyslexia who may take longer to adapt but not necessarily fail.

S8.notes.Q3: As a former dropout, I know grades don't tell the whole story. But adding high school GPA or demographics feels invasive and stigmatizing. Only first-gen or financial status might help identify hidden structural barriers.
S8.notes.Q4: If I am flagged, I need to understand why. A black box creates fear and distrust. 'Very Low' explainability is unacceptable; I would rather have fewer identified than be contacted without a clear reason.
S8.notes.Q5: Missing someone who needs help (false negative) is worse for me than unnecessary contact. We must prioritize catching everyone at risk, even if it means the overall success rate drops slightly or some unneeded emails are sent.
S8.notes.Q6: Generic mass emails feel like spam and get ignored. A personalized note showing someone cares is vital. Contact should be continuous, not just annual; struggles happen anytime.
S8.notes.Q7: It's better to send an unwanted email than to miss a student who might drop out. The intervention is supportive, not punitive, so the risk of false positives is worth taking.
S8.Q8.1: The model must ensure that students from minority backgrounds or remote areas (like me) aren't penalized for lack of local support networks. Also, I want an easy way to opt-out completely if I feel targeted.

S9.notes.Q3: Using grades is fine for small gains, but high school data feels irrelevant and invasive. Absalon tracking is okay if it helps me without revealing my health struggles.
S9.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged to trust the support offered. A black box model feels threatening when dealing with mental health issues.
S9.notes.Q5: It is unfair if the system misses students like me because of my background. I prefer catching all struggling students over perfect fairness, but missing vulnerable people is unacceptable.
S9.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel like spam. I want a personal touch that respects my situation. Continuous monitoring ensures help comes when I need it, not just once a year.
S9.notes.Q7: For generic info, be careful not to overwhelm. For personalized support, better to contact someone unnecessarily than let them fall through the cracks completely.
S9.Q8.1: The system must ensure data isn't used against me in future applications or by potential employers. There must be strict firewalls between support services and administrative record-keeping regarding my disability.
